chunks.title: dictionary entry 01: kholtu
chunks.heading: kholtu
chunks.text: Burushaski word: kholtu (part of speech: adverb). Meaning in English: today. Urdu equivalent: آج. Kashmiri equivalent: اَز /az/. Srinagar dialect: script کھولتُو, IPA /kʰolt̪u/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Je kholtu bazaarer neyba." - "I am not going to the market today." Gilgit dialect: script کھولتُو, IPA /kʰolt̪u/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Khulto haralt shuqulo." - "It is raining today."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 02: tsordi
chunks.heading: tsordi
chunks.text: Burushaski word: tsordi (part of speech: adverb). Meaning in English: tomorrow. Urdu equivalent: کل. Kashmiri equivalent: پگاہ /pagaːh/. Srinagar dialect: script ثوردی, IPA /t͡sord̪i/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Je tsordi bazaarer nibaa." - "I will go to the market tomorrow." Gilgit dialect: script ثوردی, IPA /t͡sord̪i/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Jimaly ju." - "Come tomorrow."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 03: ha
chunks.heading: ha
chunks.text: Burushaski word: ha (part of speech: noun). Meaning in English: house. Urdu equivalent: گھر. Kashmiri equivalent: گَرٕ /garɨ/. Srinagar dialect: script ہا, IPA /ha/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "A-ha Hari Parbat-ulo bila." - "My house is in Hari Parbat." Gilgit dialect: script ہا, IPA /ha/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Mulgim ha." - "Black house."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 04: hing
chunks.heading: hing
chunks.text: Burushaski word: hing (part of speech: noun). Meaning in English: door. Urdu equivalent: دروازہ. Kashmiri equivalent: دَروازہ /darvaːzɨ/. Srinagar dialect: script ہِنگ, IPA /hiŋ/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Hing yuwash." - "Open the door." Gilgit dialect: script ہِنگ, IPA /hiŋ/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Hing yuwash." - "Open the door."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 05: gatung
chunks.heading: gatung
chunks.text: Burushaski word: gatung (part of speech: noun). Meaning in English: clothes. Urdu equivalent: کپڑا / پوشاک. Kashmiri equivalent: پلو /palav/. Srinagar dialect: script گٹُونگ, IPA /gat̪uŋ/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Dasin gane gatung gitsam." - "I bought clothes for the girl." Gilgit dialect: script گٹُونگ, IPA /gat̪uŋ/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Bardum gatung." - "Red clothes."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 06: lap_chil
chunks.heading: lap_chil
chunks.text: Burushaski word: lap_chil (part of speech: noun). Meaning in English: tea. Urdu equivalent: چائے. Kashmiri equivalent: چائے /t͡ʃaːj/. Srinagar dialect: script لاپ چل, IPA /lap t͡ʃil/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Lap chil mi." - "Drink tea." Gilgit dialect: script لاپ زیل, IPA /lap ziːl/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Lap zil mi." - "Drink tea."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 07: shapik
chunks.heading: shapik
chunks.text: Burushaski word: shapik (part of speech: noun). Meaning in English: food. Urdu equivalent: کھانا. Kashmiri equivalent: ژوoٹ /t͡soːt/. Srinagar dialect: script شپِک, IPA /ʃapik/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Shapik shi." - "Eat the food." Gilgit dialect: script شبِیک, IPA /ʃabiːk/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Shabik shi." - "Eat the food."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 08: gahr
chunks.heading: gahr
chunks.text: Burushaski word: gahr (part of speech: noun). Meaning in English: marriage. Urdu equivalent: شادی. Kashmiri equivalent: کھانٛدر /kʰaːndar/. Srinagar dialect: script گہر, IPA /gaːr/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Ine gahr bila." - "It is his marriage." Gilgit dialect: script گر, IPA /gaːr/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Ine gar bila." - "It is his marriage."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 09: thala
chunks.heading: thala
chunks.text: Burushaski word: thala (part of speech: adjective). Meaning in English: slow. Urdu equivalent: آہستہ. Kashmiri equivalent: سُست /sust/. Srinagar dialect: script تھلا, IPA /tʰala/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Thala gucchar." - "Walk slowly." Gilgit dialect: script تھلا, IPA /tʰala/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Thala gucchar." - "Walk slowly."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 10: daghanum
chunks.heading: daghanum
chunks.text: Burushaski word: daghanum (part of speech: adjective). Meaning in English: fat. Urdu equivalent: موٹا. Kashmiri equivalent: وِیوٚٹھ /vjoʈʰ/. Srinagar dialect: script دغَنُم, IPA /d̪aɣanum/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Daghanum hir." - "A fat man." Gilgit dialect: script دغَنُم, IPA /d̪aɣanum/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Daghanum hir." - "A fat man."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 11: beenum
chunks.heading: beenum
chunks.text: Burushaski word: beenum (part of speech: adjective). Meaning in English: thin. Urdu equivalent: پتلا. Kashmiri equivalent: تُنک /tunk/. Srinagar dialect: script بینُم, IPA /beːnum/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Beenum dasin." - "A thin girl." Gilgit dialect: script بَینُم, IPA /beːnum/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Bainum dasin." - "A thin girl."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 12: chhagorum
chunks.heading: chhagorum
chunks.text: Burushaski word: chhagorum (part of speech: adjective). Meaning in English: cold. Urdu equivalent: ٹھنڈا. Kashmiri equivalent: یَکھ /jakʰ/. Srinagar dialect: script چھگورُم, IPA /t͡ʃʰagorum/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Chil chhagorum bila." - "The water is cold." Gilgit dialect: script چھغورُم, IPA /t͡ʃʰagorum/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Chil chaghorum bila." - "The water is cold."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 13: bayu
chunks.heading: bayu
chunks.text: Burushaski word: bayu (part of speech: noun). Meaning in English: salt. Urdu equivalent: نمک. Kashmiri equivalent: نوٗن /nuːn/. Srinagar dialect: script بایو, IPA /baju/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Bayu doro bila." - "The salt is hard." Gilgit dialect: script بیوُ, IPA /baju/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Bayu doro bila." - "The salt is hard."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 14: kasharum
chunks.heading: kasharum
chunks.text: Burushaski word: kasharum (part of speech: adjective). Meaning in English: sweet. Urdu equivalent: میٹھا. Kashmiri equivalent: موٚدُر /modur/. Srinagar dialect: script کاشرُم, IPA /kaʃarum/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Balt kasharum bila." - "The apple is sweet." Gilgit dialect: script گشنرم, IPA /kaʃarum/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Balt gashnarum bila." - "The apple is sweet."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 15: dukoil
chunks.heading: dukoil
chunks.text: Burushaski word: dukoil (part of speech: verb). Meaning in English: listen. Urdu equivalent: سنو. Kashmiri equivalent: بوزُن /boːzun/. Srinagar dialect: script دُکوئیل, IPA /d̪ukoil/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "A-dumo, dukoil!" - "O girl, listen!" Gilgit dialect: script دُکوئیل, IPA /d̪ukoil/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "A-dumo, dukoil!" - "O girl, listen!"

chunks.title: dictionary entry 16: roo
chunks.heading: roo
chunks.text: Burushaski word: roo (part of speech: verb). Meaning in English: come. Urdu equivalent: آؤ. Kashmiri equivalent: یُن /jun/. Srinagar dialect: script رُو, IPA /ruː/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Khole roo!" - "Come here!" Gilgit dialect: script رُو, IPA /ruː/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Khole ru!" - "Come here!"

chunks.title: dictionary entry 17: ney
chunks.heading: ney
chunks.text: Burushaski word: ney (part of speech: verb). Meaning in English: go. Urdu equivalent: جاؤ. Kashmiri equivalent: گَژھُن /gat͡sʰun/. Srinagar dialect: script نے, IPA /ne/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Bazaarer ney!" - "Go to the market!" Gilgit dialect: script مِ, IPA /mi/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Bazaarer mi!" - "Go to the market!"

chunks.title: dictionary entry 18: shuwa
chunks.heading: shuwa
chunks.text: Burushaski word: shuwa (part of speech: adjective). Meaning in English: good. Urdu equivalent: اچھا. Kashmiri equivalent: جان /d͡ʒaːn/. Srinagar dialect: script شوا, IPA /ʃuwa/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Shuwa ba." - "I am good." Gilgit dialect: script شُوا, IPA /ʃuwa/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Shuwa ba." - "I am good."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 19: dalkash
chunks.heading: dalkash
chunks.text: Burushaski word: dalkash (part of speech: adjective). Meaning in English: very good. Urdu equivalent: بہت اچھا. Kashmiri equivalent: واریاہ جان /vaːrjaːh d͡ʒaːn/. Srinagar dialect: script دلکَش, IPA /d̪alkaʃ/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Ine dalkash bai." - "He is very good." Gilgit dialect: script دلتَس, IPA /d̪altas/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Ine daltas bai." - "He is very good."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 20: shukum
chunks.heading: shukum
chunks.text: Burushaski word: shukum (part of speech: adjective). Meaning in English: beautiful. Urdu equivalent: خوبصورت. Kashmiri equivalent: خوٗبصوٗرت /xuːbsuːrat/. Srinagar dialect: script شُکُم, IPA /ʃukum/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Dasin shukum bo." - "The girl is beautiful." Gilgit dialect: script شُکُم, IPA /ʃukum/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Dasin shukum bo." - "The girl is beautiful."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 21: tum
chunks.heading: tum
chunks.text: Burushaski word: tum (part of speech: noun). Meaning in English: tree. Urdu equivalent: درخت. Kashmiri equivalent: کُل /kul/. Srinagar dialect: script ٹوم, IPA /t̪om/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Tom eikhan bila." - "The tree is tall." Gilgit dialect: script تُم, IPA /t̪um/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Tum eikhan bila." - "The tree is tall."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 22: giram
chunks.heading: giram
chunks.text: Burushaski word: giram (part of speech: noun). Meaning in English: neighborhood. Urdu equivalent: محلہ. Kashmiri equivalent: مَحلہٕ /mahla/. Srinagar dialect: script گِرم, IPA /giram/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Giram-ulo." - "In the neighborhood." Gilgit dialect: script گِرم, IPA /giram/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Giram-ulo." - "In the neighborhood."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 23: birdi
chunks.heading: birdi
chunks.text: Burushaski word: birdi (part of speech: noun). Meaning in English: earth. Urdu equivalent: زمین. Kashmiri equivalent: زٔمیٖن /zəmiːn/. Srinagar dialect: script بِردِ, IPA /bird̪i/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Birdi-ulo." - "On the earth." Gilgit dialect: script بِردِ, IPA /bird̪i/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Birdi-ulo." - "On the earth."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 24: ayash
chunks.heading: ayash
chunks.text: Burushaski word: ayash (part of speech: noun). Meaning in English: sky. Urdu equivalent: آسمان. Kashmiri equivalent: آسمان /aːsmaːn/. Srinagar dialect: script اَیَش, IPA /ajaʃ/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Ayash yater bila." - "The sky is above." Gilgit dialect: script اَیَش, IPA /ajaʃ/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Ayash yater bila." - "The sky is above."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 25: thanum
chunks.heading: thanum
chunks.text: Burushaski word: thanum (part of speech: adjective). Meaning in English: tall, big. Urdu equivalent: لمبا. Kashmiri equivalent: تھود /tʰod/. Srinagar dialect: script تھانُم, IPA /tʰanum/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Thanum tom." - "A tall tree." Gilgit dialect: script غُسنُم / تھانُم, IPA /tʰanum/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Thanum / ghusnum tom." - "A tall / long tree."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 26: ghusnum
chunks.heading: ghusnum
chunks.text: Burushaski word: ghusnum (part of speech: adjective). Meaning in English: long, tall. Urdu equivalent: لمبا. Kashmiri equivalent: جیوٹھ /d͡ʒjuːʈʰ/. Srinagar dialect: script غُسنُم, IPA /ɣusnum/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Ghusnum ghuying." - "Long hair." Gilgit dialect: script غُسنُم, IPA /ɣusnum/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Ghusnum ghuying." - "Long hair."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 27: meedum
chunks.heading: meedum
chunks.text: Burushaski word: meedum (part of speech: noun). Meaning in English: our body. Urdu equivalent: ہمارا جسم. Kashmiri equivalent: میون جِسم /mjoːn d͡ʒism/. Srinagar dialect: script مِیڈِم, IPA /miːd̪um/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Meedum daltas bila." - "Our body is beautiful." Gilgit dialect: script مِیڈِم, IPA /miːd̪um/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Midim daltas bila." - "Our body is beautiful."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 28: uiras
chunks.heading: uiras
chunks.text: Burushaski word: uiras (part of speech: verb). Meaning in English: to die. Urdu equivalent: مرنا. Kashmiri equivalent: مَرُن /marun/. Srinagar dialect: script ویرَس, IPA /uiras/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Ine uirabai." - "He is dying." Gilgit dialect: script اویَس, IPA /uiras/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Ine uyasbai." - "He is dying."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 29: mey
chunks.heading: mey
chunks.text: Burushaski word: mey (part of speech: pronoun). Meaning in English: we. Urdu equivalent: ہم. Kashmiri equivalent: أسۍ /əsʲ/. Srinagar dialect: script مے, IPA /me/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Mey burusho ba." - "We are Burusho." Gilgit dialect: script مِ, IPA /mi/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Mi burusho ba." - "We are Burusho."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 30: um
chunks.heading: um
chunks.text: Burushaski word: um (part of speech: pronoun). Meaning in English: you. Urdu equivalent: تم. Kashmiri equivalent: ژٕ /t͡sɨ/. Srinagar dialect: script اُم, IPA /um/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Um be hal be?" - "How are you?" Gilgit dialect: script اُم, IPA /um/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Um be hal be?" - "How are you?"

chunks.title: dictionary entry 31: jey
chunks.heading: jey
chunks.text: Burushaski word: jey (part of speech: pronoun). Meaning in English: me. Urdu equivalent: میں. Kashmiri equivalent: بٔ /bɨ/. Srinagar dialect: script جے, IPA /d͡ʒe/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Jey Burusho ba." - "I am a Burusho." Gilgit dialect: script جے, IPA /d͡ʒe/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Je Burusho ba." - "I am a Burusho."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 32: giretas
chunks.heading: giretas
chunks.text: Burushaski word: giretas (part of speech: verb). Meaning in English: play. Urdu equivalent: کھیلنا. Kashmiri equivalent: گِنٛدون /gindun/. Srinagar dialect: script گیرِیتَس, IPA /giret̪as/. Example in Srinagar dialect: "Gushingants giretas." - "The women are dancing." Gilgit dialect: script گیرِیتَس, IPA /giret̪as/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Gushingants giritas." - "The women are dancing."

chunks.title: dictionary entry 33: urutas
chunks.heading: urutas

chunks.heading: gartas

chunks.heading: demilas

Example in Srinagar dialect: "Demilas." - "To hear / listen." Gilgit dialect: script اِمیلَس, IPA /imilas/. Example in Gilgit dialect: "Imilas." - "To hear / listen."

chunks.title: Srinagar Burushaski report
chunks.heading: Srinagar Burushaski — Research Report
chunks.text:
Compiled 2026-09-26 from 10 parallel research passes for the Burushaski Digital Archive (https://aazimameen1.in/). Everything below is sourced; uncertain items are flagged.

---

chunks.title: Srinagar Burushaski report
chunks.heading: 1. History and origins
chunks.text: The Srinagar Burusho community descends from princes of Hunza and Nagar who migrated with families and attendants from the Hunza and Nagar valleys (now Gilgit-Baltistan) to Kashmir in the late 19th century, during the Dogra period. Sources disagree on the exact year: Musavir Ahmed (EJECS) says the elders migrated in 1888; another paper (IJSR) dates it to 1891 onwards, citing "political upheavals" in Hunza and Nagar — consistent with the December 1891 British–Dogra campaign against Hunza-Nagar (the Anglo-Brusho War). Treat 1888–1891 as approximate.

chunks.title: Srinagar Burushaski report
chunks.heading: 1. History and origins
chunks.text:
unza and Nagar — consistent with the December 1891 British–Dogra campaign against Hunza-Nagar (the Anglo-Brusho War). Treat 1888–1891 as approximate.

Community oral history (The Citizen, 2023) names the ancestors as Raja Azur Khan and Rehan Ali Shah, fleeing to Srinagar after losing to the British in 1891. Note: historical records of the 1891 campaign name the actual Mirs as Safdar Ali Khan of Hunza and Zafar Zahid Khan of Nagar, so the oral-history names are worth flagging rather than asserting.

On arrival, the Dogra ruler granted them several hundred kanals of land plus a fixed state pension. They settled southeast of Hari Parbat fort in the Makhdoom Sahib area, in what became known as Botraj Mohalla (also "Mohalla Azur Khan").

**Sources:** EJECS (https://www.ejecs.org/index.php/JECS/article/download/51/33) · IJSR (https://www.ijsr.net/archive/v5i1/NOV153102.pdf) · The Citizen (https://www.thecitizen.in/life/have-you-heard-burushaski-897505) · Wikipedia Burusho people (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burusho_people)

---

chunks.title: Srinagar Burushaski report
chunks.heading: 2. Demographics and endangerment
chunks.text:
- **Speakers:** ~300–350, in ~35–40 families. The Census of India does not enumerate Burushaski separately. No published count younger than ~2023; treat as working figure.
- **Where:** Core is Mohalla Azur Khan (Botraj Mohalla), Kathi Darwaza, foothills of Hari Parbat; satellite households in Tral, Batamaloo, Bemina. Community is Shia, holds ST status, calls the language *miśāski* ("our language").
- **Status:** UNESCO's Atlas rates Burushaski (whole language) as "Vulnerable" — but that reflects ~120,000 speakers in Pakistan, not the Srinagar enclave. Whether UNESCO scores the Srinagar variety separately is uncertain. On vitality measures, the Srinagar group scores very low: ~350 people among 7+ million, no written form, no institutional/media/government support, parent group in Pakistan cut off since 1947.

chunks.title: Srinagar Burushaski report
chunks.heading: 2. Demographics and endangerment
chunks.text:
cores very low: ~350 people among 7+ million, no written form, no institutional/media/government support, parent group in Pakistan cut off since 1947.
- **Transmission:** Still functioning but narrowing. Mushtaq's 2015–16 fieldwork (76 respondents): Burushaski used with grandparents (94–98%), parents (92%), spouses (72%), children (85%). Home is the last stand — zero use in education and workplace. Age-cohort breakdowns were not published (gap).

**Sources:** Munshi 2006 (https://www.academia.edu/728801/...) · Sheikh & Jan phonological study (https://selindia.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/Burushaski-cleaned.pdf) · New Indian Express (https://www.newindianexpress.com/magazine/2025/Oct/26/echoes-of-the-mountains) · Mushtaq IJSR 2016 (https://www.ijsr.net/archive/v5i3/NOV162329.pdf)

---

chunks.title: Srinagar Burushaski report
chunks.heading: 3. What makes the Srinagar dialect distinct
chunks.text:
Srinagar Burushaski (Jammu & Kashmir Burushaski, JKB) descends primarily from the **Nagar** dialect; after ~120 years of isolation it is "systematically different" from the Pakistan varieties.

- **Vowel syncopation — unique to JKB.** Medial unstressed [u] is deleted: *bur.śa:s.ki* 'Burushaski' vs Nagar/Hunza *bu.ru.śas.ki*; *t̪ap.mo* 'at night' vs *t̪a.pu.-mo*; *ċham.ni* 'hungry' vs *ċha.mi.ni*. No Pakistan dialect shows this — it is the diagnostic feature.
- **Monophthongization.** Sequences like [eu] collapse to [e:] or [o:]: *be:r.ma:n* 'how much' vs Nagar *beu.ru.ma:n*.
- **Tone.** Described as "low toned" relative to the Pakistan dialects, aligning with the simplified vowel system.

chunks.title: Srinagar Burushaski report
chunks.heading: 3. What makes the Srinagar dialect distinct
chunks.text:
'how much' vs Nagar *beu.ru.ma:n*.
- **Tone.** Described as "low toned" relative to the Pakistan dialects, aligning with the simplified vowel system.
- **Contact signature.** JKB is the most contact-affected variety: heavily influenced by Kashmiri, Urdu, Hindi. Diagnostic: Urdu loans ending in [a] keep [a] in JKB (*ja:la* 'cobweb', *ayina* 'mirror') vs [o] in Hunza/Nagar (*ja:lo*, *ayino*).

It retains Burushaski agglutinative morphology, echo-formations, and a rich consonant inventory (stops, retroflexes, uvulars, aspirates).

**Sources:** Munshi 2006 (academia.edu) · Sheikh & Jan (selindia.org) · Wikipedia Burushaski (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burushaski)

---

chunks.title: Srinagar Burushaski report
chunks.heading: 4. Kashmiri and Urdu influence
chunks.text:
- **Urdu** influence comes via second-language speakers — state official language, medium of instruction, local media/TV (Hindi via TV too).
- **Kashmiri** influence comes through native Kashmiri speakers in daily spoken interaction.
- The community's own name "Botraj" comes from Kashmiri *Raj* ("king") — a history of Kashmiri labeling.
- **Domain split (Mushtaq, n=76):** Burushaski dominates home (~90%), mosque (~85%), market with fellow Burushos (~70%); but zero in education/workplace (Urdu ~58–83%, Kashmiri ~9–29%, English). With non-Burushos at the market, Urdu is used 100%. Repertoire: Burushaski + Balti + Kashmiri + Urdu + English; children pick up Urdu "from the environment," Kashmiri at school.

chunks.title: Srinagar Burushaski report
chunks.heading: 4. Kashmiri and Urdu influence
chunks.text:
rket, Urdu is used 100%. Repertoire: Burushaski + Balti + Kashmiri + Urdu + English; children pick up Urdu "from the environment," Kashmiri at school.
- Specific documented loanword examples or code-switched utterances are **not** in accessible online sources — Munshi's dissertation/book aren't freely online. Don't publish invented examples.

**Sources:** Munshi 2006 · Mushtaq IJSR v5i1/v5i3 · Wikipedia

---

chunks.title: Srinagar Burushaski report
chunks.heading: 5. Srinagar vs Yasin (Werchikwar)
chunks.text:
Srinagar Burushaski descends from Nagar/Hunza stock, so its relationship to Yasin mirrors the broader Hunza–Nagar vs Yasin divergence. Yasin (Khowar exonym Werchikwar) is the most divergent Pakistani variety — difficult intelligibility with Hunza–Nagar, sometimes treated as a distinct language, regarded by its own speakers as "pure" Burushaski.

Sharpest contrast: Yasin is the *least* affected by neighboring languages (bilingual in Khowar); Srinagar is the *most* contact-affected (Kashmiri/Urdu/Hindi). Lorimer (1937) documents Khowar contact signatures in Yasin (borrowed imperfect auxiliary *avstam* "I was doing"; dative suffix *-a/-van*).

The full Srinagar↔Yasin contrast table is in Munshi's book Chapter 7 (paywalled). No open-access word-by-word Srinagar↔Yasin comparison exists publicly.

**Sources:** Brill (https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/isbn/9789004387898/html?lang=en) · Stanford SearchWorks (https://searchworks.stanford.edu/view/12889902) · Lorimer 1937 (pahar.in) · JoLR 2019 (https://jolr.ru/files/(273)jlr2019-17-3-4(263-284).pdf) · INFLIBNET e-PG Pathshala (https://epgp.inflibnet.ac.in/epgpdata/uploads/epgp_content/S000022LS/P001756/M023420/ET/1506322409Lings-P7-M28.pdf)

chunks.title: Srinagar Burushaski report
chunks.heading: 7. Documentation efforts
chunks.text:
Srinagar Burushaski is one of the best-documented regional varieties relative to its size, though still thin:

1. **Munshi 2006** — *Jammu and Kashmir Burushaski: Language, Language Contact, and Change*, UT Austin dissertation (handle http://hdl.handle.net/2152/2777). Notes no prior study of the J&K variety existed.
2. **Munshi 2019** — *Srinagar Burushaski: A Descriptive and Comparative Account with Analyzed Texts*, Brill Vol. 11 (305 pp.). Full structural description + analyzed texts; digital corpus at the UNT Digital Library (access terms unverified).
3. **Munshi 2010** — "Contact-induced language change in a trilingual context," *Diachronica* 27(1): 32–72 (DOI 10.1075/dia.27.1.02mun).
4. **Sabba Mushtaq** — sociolinguistic vitality studies, IJSR v5i1 and v5i3.

chunks.heading: 7. Documentation efforts
chunks.text:

4. **Sabba Mushtaq** — sociolinguistic vitality studies, IJSR v5i1 and v5i3.
5. **Aejaz Mohammed Sheikh & Saima Jan** — "A Phonological Study of Burushaski Spoken in Srinagar," *वाक्मंथन* Vol.1 Issue I (SEL India); full phonemic inventory + minimal pairs from Jan–Feb 2015 fieldwork in Mohalla Azur Khan (https://selindia.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/Burushaski-cleaned.pdf).
6. **Shahnaz Hunzia, *Burushaski–Urdu Dictionary*, 2009** — main published lexicon, but Hunza-based, not Srinagar-specific.

**Gaps:** No public Srinagar-dialect recordings in ELAR, PARADISEC, or other open archives — only the UNT corpus (access uncertain). Grierson's *Linguistic Survey of India* doesn't cover the Srinagar variety specifically.

chunks.title: Srinagar Burushaski report
chunks.heading: 9. Oral literature
chunks.text:
- **Richest source:** Munshi's UNT "Burushaski Language Resource" — explicitly a digital collection of Burushaski oral literature (https://digital.library.unt.edu/explore/collections/BURUS/), built from Srinagar fieldwork (~2002) plus Nagar/Hunza/Yasin comparisons. Item-level contents unverified (403 on fetch) — *uncertain* if fully public.
- **Munshi's Brill grammar (2019)** includes "analyzed texts" — transcribed, glossed Srinagar speech. Likely the only published connected Srinagar discourse.
- **"Okus bokus" children's rhyme** — Munshi's Kashmir Observer piece (2020) documents the counting-out game rhyme with possible Burushaski remnants (https://kashmirobserver.net/2020/08/18/the-mystery-of-okus-bokus/).

chunks.heading: 9. Oral literature
chunks.text:
ce (2020) documents the counting-out game rhyme with possible Burushaski remnants (https://kashmirobserver.net/2020/08/18/the-mystery-of-okus-bokus/).
- **Already on the site:** "An Intelligent Old Man," "Um Ba Khudaye," "Folk Song (Standard)," "Folk Song (Alternative)" — attribution and dialect basis unclear; verify whether Srinagar-recorded or adapted from Pakistan material.
- **Caveat:** The big folklore corpora (Lorimer 1935–38, Berger 1998, van Skyhawk's Kisar epic, Tiffou's *Hunza Proverbs*) all record Hunza/Nagar/Yasin — not Srinagar. Conflating them misrepresents the dialect the archive claims to document.

**Bottom line:** Almost nothing published is specifically Srinagar oral literature beyond Munshi's corpus/texts and the Okus-bokus discussion. Best leads: Munshi's UNT collection and the Khan/Fatima recording project.

**From Munshi 2006 (everyday speech §2.2):** *ph iś et̪i!* "Pee, pee, pee!" · *jaa jigaran menan bai?* "Who is my dear one?" · *bate-re d̪am d̪i: bia?* "Is the rice cooked/ready?" **Numbers 1–10 (Munshi Table 5.3, JKB; vary by noun class):** 1 *hin/han/hik*, 2 *alt̪an/alt̪ac/alt̪o*, 3 *isken/usko/iski*, 4 *valt̪o/valt̪i*, 5 *chund̪o/chind̪i*, 6 *miśind̪o/miśind̪i*, 7 uncertain (table garbled; Hunza *t̪ali* unconfirmed for Srinagar), 8 *alt̪ambo/alt̪ambi*, 9 *hunco/hunti*, 10 *t̪o:rmo/t̪o:rmi*. Caveat: speakers frequently replace higher numerals with Urdu loans (*d̪o*, *pã:ć*, *d̪as*…).

**Common verbs (Munshi Table 5.5):** *et̪-as* 'to do', *manaas* 'to become', *gucharas* 'to walk', *şi-* 'to eat', *ga:rc-* 'to run', *girat̪-* 'to dance', *ni-* 'to go', *żu-* 'to come', *girm-* 'to write', *d̪Vyil-* 'to listen'.

chunks.heading: What this means for the archive (recommendations)
chunks.text:
1. **A "Srinagar Dialect" page** — the archive's unique claim. The vowel-syncopation feature, the *miśa:ski* endonym, the 1891 story, and the ~300-speaker figure are its strongest content. Nobody else is telling this story online in one place.
2. **Verify the Collections' dialect basis** — the stories/songs on the site need provenance labels (Srinagar-recorded vs adapted from Pakistan material), or the archive risks misrepresenting its own dialect focus.
3. **Highest-value dictionary additions:** the numeral table (with the Urdu-borrowing caveat), the possessed kinship paradigms, the 5 everyday speech sentences, the kinship terms — all directly sourced from Munshi (2006).
